catalog_quote: Enrico 1991:111-121 (as carried by StressTyp2): "In level tone words, the pattern is simple. The final syllable gets main stress and all alternates before it get secondary stress. When there are both high and low tones in a word, the pattern is more complicated. The last high tone gets main stress. All alternates before it and the last syllable and alternates before it get secondary stress." | de Lacy 2002:23, (32): "(32) lists a number of languages in which tone is the primary factor in determining the position of stress ... b. Stress the rightmost high-toned syllable, else the rightmost syllable Golin Bunn & Bunn (1970), Bunn (1974) Masset Haida Enrico (1991 : 111ff)"

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'weight' (unbounded, tone-driven: main stress on the rightmost high-toned syllable, else the final syllable) is correct for Masset Haida and is supported three ways in copies we hold: (i) the StressTyp2-carried Enrico 1991:111-121 passage (verbatim in the held StressTyp2 dump), (ii) de Lacy 2002:23 ex.(32b) and de Lacy 2007 ex.(26), both confirmed verbatim in held author-copy PDFs, and (iii) -- not yet used by the record -- Enrico's own open sketch, Enrico 1989 'The Haida Language' p.225 item 6, 'Word stress in Masset has the last high-tone syllable in the word (if there is one) main-stressed, otherwise the word-final syllable is main-stressed'. sources.citation: Enrico, John (1986). Tone and Nucleus in Masset Haida. Unpublished typescript, May 1986, ca. 26 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item HAM975En1986c, Fairbanks.
sources.tag: likely states tone; not yet obtained
sources.note: ANLA record quotes the introduction: pitch and syllable structure are related in all Haida dialects; for Masset 'certain facts of length follow from pitch rather than vice versa and.. pitch is syllable tone'; the nucleus (Clements & Keyser) is the unit assigned tone; 'Masset high tone is assigned at strata 1-3.. strata 2 and 3 are cyclic.. predictable low tone is assigned non-cyclically and therefore postlexically. Only low tone on underived heavy syllables is given in underlying representation.'.

sources.citation: Enrico, John (1982). Adjacent Syllable Nuclei in Masset Haida. Unpublished paper, ca. 44 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item HAM975En1982a, Fairbanks.
sources.tag: likely states tone; not yet obtained
sources.note: ANLA abstract: 'Preparatory to describing a unique way in which one language -- Masset Haida -- treats adjacent syllable nuclei in the stem, the vowel and pitch systems and two types of lexical syllable boundary are described. The MH treatment of adjacent syllable nuclei is then explained in terms of three conspiracies and it is shown that a formal description requires a hierarchical syllable-structure notation..' (coalescence of adjacent vowels and glides).
